title: Transformed Array
notes:
## Intuition

Walking step by step works, but each walk can take up to 100 steps and loops around the array many times. Moving `nums[i]` steps from index `i` around a circle of `n` cells always ends at index `i + nums[i]` reduced modulo `n`, so each landing index can be computed in one line. A value of `0` lands on `i` itself, so the same formula also covers that rule.

## Approach

1. Let `n` be the length of `nums` and make an empty `result` of the same length.
2. For each index `i`, compute `landing = ((i + nums[i]) % n + n) % n`. The first `%` removes whole laps; adding `n` and taking `%` again turns a negative remainder into the matching index.
3. Set `result[i] = nums[landing]`, reading from the untouched input.
4. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, -2, 1, 1]`, `n = 4`.

- `i = 0`: `0 + 3 = 3`, so `landing = 3` and `result[0] = 1`.
- `i = 1`: `1 - 2 = -1`; `-1 % 4` is `-1` in JavaScript, and `(-1 + 4) % 4 = 3`, so `result[1] = 1`.
- `i = 2`: `2 + 1 = 3`, so `result[2] = 1`.
- `i = 3`: `3 + 1 = 4`, which wraps to `0`, so `result[3] = 3`.

The answer is `[1, 1, 1, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one constant-time index calculation per element.
- Space: O(n) for `result` (O(1) besides the output).

## Pitfalls

- In JavaScript, Java and C, `%` keeps the sign of the left operand, so `(i + nums[i]) % n` can be negative; add `n` and reduce again.
- Do not write the answers into `nums` while you go: with `[1, -1, 5]`, index `1` must read the original `1` at index `0`, not the `-1` written there.
- Steps can be far more than `n` (100 steps on an array of length 3); reducing modulo `n` handles any number of laps.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `result` | the transformed array being built |
| `i` | the index whose walk is being computed |
| `landing` | the index where the walk from `i` ends |

narration.2: n is the number of cells in the circle.
narration.3: result is a separate array, so every walk reads the original values of nums.
narration.4: Work out each index's walk on its own.
narration.5: i + nums[i] is where the walk would end on an endless line; % n removes whole laps, and adding n before the second % turns a negative remainder into a real index.
narration.6: The value where the walk stops becomes result[i]; when nums[i] is 0 the walk stops at i itself.
narration.8: Every index has its transformed value, so return the new array.
